By Courtney Gould

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has just stepped up, officially confirming the news we've been reporting all morning — the underlying deficit is $6 lower than the $28.3b initially forecast in May.

He credits this to a decrease in payments (down $1.4b) and an increase in receipts (up $4.6b).

Chalmers says the improvements are not because and improvement in commodity prices or because more people are paying tax on wages.

"In fact mining profits came in lower than what was anticipated," he says.

"It is overwhelmingly from higher super and investor income than what we anticipated in the Treasury's forecasts in May."

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher credits the improved result to spending less across aged care, child care, the pharmaceutical benefits scheme (PBS) and "a couple of national partnership payments".

By Courtney Gould

Hi friends. Courtney Gould joining you on the blog for the rest of the day.

We're standing by for a press conference from Jim Chalmers and Katy Gallagher, where they'll be walking us through the final budget outcome.

As Josh has flagged already on the blog, it's expected budget bottom line will be $6 billion lower than the $28.3 billion deficit forecast in the budget in May.

I'll bring you all the highlights as they roll in, so stick around!

By Joshua Boscaini

Jonno Duniam says the Coalition has been engaged with the Parliamentary Budget Office over its migration policy.

The Coalition is expected to release its migration policy ahead of the next sitting week in October, after One Nation released its policy and Labor announced an overhaul to the system,

Speaking to News24, the shadow home affairs minister has indicated the Coalition will target dependents of student or temporary visa holders.

"The number that we do arrive at as part of our policy we need to make sure that that number make a economic contribution. That they aren't attached just people who are attached to someone else who is here on a student or other temporary visa as a secondary visa applicant," Duniam says.

By Joshua Boscaini

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has raised issued with the government's plan to limit backpacker numbers as part of a crackdown on migration.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced a shake up of the migration system this month, which included limits on backpacker stays and a tightening of visa rules for international students.

Speaking to News24, Joyce says working holiday makers are needed in the regions and the government is targeting the wrong group of migrants.

"Where we actually need the people they've actually making it incredibly hard to get the people, and where we don't need the people they're still pouring in," Joyce says.

By Lexie Jeuniewic

Liberal frontbencher James Paterson says Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is stoking disproportionate fear over the OpenAI data breach.

As we've been reporting, OpenAI disclosed this month that one of its autonomous agents gained unauthorised access to Medicare health statistics portal held by Services Australia by finding a security workaround in June.

The government has since launched a taskforce to forensically investigate the incident.

Paterson tells Channel Nine while the breach is of "concern", the government should treat it as a "free warning" and an opportunity to get the tech giants on side.

"We're going to need to attract the best AI technology in the world to Australia to make sure we have access to it, and we are going to need to make sure that we put in place appropriate guardrails and oversight of these AI companies so that we do have a better idea of what they're doing and so risks like
